Seventeen comments

The Grinders

A slip jig culled from Raven’s “English Country Dance Tunes” by the Durham-based band Horseplay and featured on their album “Roughshod” (I’ve entered that in the “Recordings” section).
It’s a sturdy English jig - in other words, liable to dispense with quavers where a dotted crotchet will do - but I think a good tune all told.

↳ Posted by nicholas on November 12th, 2006.

The Grinders

The final crotchet in the sheet music should have been a high D, not a low one.
It’s one of those tunes that can be played in the single major octave early Northumbrian smallpipers had to make do with.

↳ Posted by nicholas on November 12th, 2006.

Terry Hi Ho The Grinder

Setting #3 is transcribed from Irish Flute Tunes:
http://irishflute.podbean.com/2012/01/08/terry-hi-ho-the-grinder-slip-jig/
(great site BTW, in case there’s a flute learner out there who really doesn’t know it)

The order of the (two) parts is just the other way round. As it is in O’Neill’s, too.
I like this setting especially because of the occasional drop to the low D. Boom.

The Grinders, X:7

Called Tobias the Grinder in the Winder manuscripts
(www,andyhornby.net/Winders.html)
There is a great song to it.

Perhaps grinding is a reference to millers adulterating their flour?

The Grinders or More Grist to the Mill.

Search all the world high and low, many a freak you’ll be finding,
What do you think’s all the go? by the Hokey it’s nothing but grinding.

Terry, Io, io, Scandal the devil can’t bind her,
the world is all “How came you so?”and every profession turned Grinder.

for they know if they let you grow well, you’ll die soon enough of starvation.

Re: The Grinders

“Attributed to piper Patsy Touhey”

Just to be clear, the second setting of this tune in Muisv of Ireland came from the playing of Patsy Touhey, rather than being his composition.

↳ Posted by Nigel Gatherer on March 13th, 2026.

Re: The Grinders

Ah, the “attributions” in ONMI are a source of contention, as O’Neill remarked in his writings. A person given as the source may have actually learned it from another member of the Chicago fraternity, which led to yet more squabbling. They were really at each other’s throats eventually…

But being listed as a source in ONMI was almost always understood to mean the musician was the source of a traditional tune; the exceptions would be John McFadden and Edward Cronin, who composed a few numbers, some of which we still play - Queen of the Fair, and I think the Bantry hornpipe? Among others.

Looking at Touhey’s Terry you can almost hear what he would have played, if you’re familiar with his recordings. Plenty of room for the “triplet with the top hand,” AC#A, and probably a cran on the E.
